l: Eugenia's accident, From Sand Hill to Pine, By this time the sun had left the burning ledge of the Eureka Company, and the s
s: Eugenia gets off the coach and wanders near the spring before falling down a ravine. Her fall delays Neworth, and the track made by it later helps Parkhurst identify disturbed ground containing quartz and gold.

l: the strike on Eureka mountain, From Sand Hill to Pine, By this time the sun had left the burning ledge of the Eureka Company, and the s
s: Parkhurst discovers gold in a pocket of decomposed quartz near the spring after widening a crack with his clasp knife. The partners prospect the area and determine that the discovery is a major strike.

l: the mining claim at the spring, From Sand Hill to Pine, By this time the sun had left the burning ledge of the Eureka Company, and the s
s: The mining claim at the spring is located by the partners after Parkhurst's discovery. They post a Notice of Location and begin excavating and testing the ground, although the spring was known to others and the validity of their work is initially uncertain.

l: the gold, From Sand Hill to Pine, By this time the sun had left the burning ledge of the Eureka Company, and the s
s: Gold is found in a small pocket of decomposed quartz near the spring. Further prospecting reveals enough gold and promise to exceed the partners' most hopeful expectations.

l: quartz, From Sand Hill to Pine, By this time the sun had left the burning ledge of the Eureka Company, and the s
s: Quartz is found near the spring in decomposed form and throughout the seepage beneath the hillside. Parkhurst connects the word "quartz" to Eugenia's note through the sequence gills, pints, and quarts.

l: water, From Sand Hill to Pine, By this time the sun had left the burning ledge of the Eureka Company, and the s
s: Water is scarce and valuable at the mining camp, and the partners' water-carrying duties require hard work. The spring's past or present water action appears to have caused erosion and exposed the quartz and gold.

l: the Notice of Location, From Sand Hill to Pine, By this time the sun had left the burning ledge of the Eureka Company, and the s
s: The partners pin a Notice of Location to a pine by the road bank beside the spring. Stage passengers see the notice when the coach passes that afternoon.

l: Eugenia's note to Parkhurst, From Sand Hill to Pine, By this time the sun had left the burning ledge of the Eureka Company, and the s
s: Eugenia's note is addressed on the back to "Jack" and says, "I want you to believe that I, at least, respect and honor your honest, manly calling, and when you strike it rich, as you surely will, I hope you will sometimes think of Jill." Parkhurst mistakes "Jill" for a reference to a gill of whiskey, while Bray recognizes it as Eugenia's remembrance of him and uses the note to explain the quartz discovery.

l: From Sand Hill to Pine, From Sand Hill to Pine, That night Bray slept but little.
s: Edmund Bray travels to San Francisco to thank Eugenia Neworth for her note and explain why he did not answer it sooner. After Eugenia initially treats him coldly, Bray enters the Neworths' garden by climbing the wall, and they clarify the misunderstandings surrounding her note and its delivery to the spring. Eugenia then directs Bray to call properly on her father, who is interested in the mines on Eureka ledge. Bray continues visiting San Francisco and eventually enters a new partnership with Eugenia, whom he says made the first strike on Eureka mountain.

l: Edward Bray, From Sand Hill to Pine, That night Bray slept but little.
s: Edmund Bray goes to San Francisco intending to seek Eugenia Neworth and thank her for her note. After Eugenia initially passes him coldly, he sends her note back with an explanation, then climbs into the Neworths' garden to speak with her. He later calls properly at the Neworth residence, visits repeatedly, and eventually enters a new partnership with Eugenia.

l: Eugenia Neworth, From Sand Hill to Pine, That night Bray slept but little.
s: Eugenia Neworth wrote the note that Bray found at the spring and arranged for a schoolboy to deliver it and wait until Bray claimed it. She explains that she expected Bray to acknowledge the note and later invites him to call on her properly. She and Bray resolve their misunderstanding, and she becomes his new partner.

l: the Neworth family, From Sand Hill to Pine, That night Bray slept but little.
s: The Neworth family lives in a palatial residence on Rincon Hill in San Francisco, with a garden protected by a high wall. Their earlier discourtesy toward Bray makes him hesitate before approaching the house.

l: Eugenia's father, Mr. Neworth, From Sand Hill to Pine, That night Bray slept but little.
s: Eugenia's father is a well-known investor who regrets not becoming better acquainted with Bray during their brief earlier interview. He is exceedingly interested in the mines on Eureka ledge and is willing to receive Bray when Bray calls at the house.

l: San Francisco, From Sand Hill to Pine, That night Bray slept but little.
s: San Francisco is where Eugenia lives with her family and where Bray goes to seek her. Bray visits the city frequently after their meeting and eventually does not return to his old partners.

l: Eureka mountain, From Sand Hill to Pine, That night Bray slept but little.
s: Eureka mountain is the place associated with Bray's mining activities and with his earlier meeting with Eugenia. Bray later says that Eugenia made the first strike on Eureka mountain.

l: Eureka ledge, From Sand Hill to Pine, That night Bray slept but little.
s: Eureka ledge contains mines in which Eugenia's father is exceedingly interested. Bray's affairs include purchasing machinery for a new claim connected with his mining work.

l: the spring, From Sand Hill to Pine, That night Bray slept but little.
s: The spring is where Eugenia had a schoolboy leave her note for Bray. Bray went there for water, but failed to notice the note while searching around the mountain, and one of his partners found it instead.

l: Eugenia's note to Parkhurst, From Sand Hill to Pine, That night Bray slept but little.
s: Eugenia's note was intended for Bray and was left at the spring by a schoolboy instructed to wait until Bray arrived. Bray did not see it because he was searching elsewhere, and he later returns it to Eugenia with thanks and an explanation for his delayed acknowledgment.

l: Bray's mining claim, From Sand Hill to Pine, That night Bray slept but little.
s: Bray is arranging the purchase of machinery for his new mining claim. His mining affairs provide him with a possible means of gaining access to Eugenia's father.

l: Bray and Eugenia's new partnership, From Sand Hill to Pine, That night Bray slept but little.
s: After Bray makes repeated visits to San Francisco, he enters into a new partnership with Eugenia. He says that she made the first strike on Eureka mountain.

l: the strike on Eureka mountain, From Sand Hill to Pine, That night Bray slept but little.
s: The strike on Eureka mountain is credited by Bray to Eugenia, who made the first strike. This description marks her as the partner who initiated the new partnership's opportunity.

l: From Sand Hill to Pine, From Sand Hill to Pine, Mr. Bilson's Housekeeper
s: After Joshua Bilson’s wife dies, he hires Miss Euphemia Trotter as housekeeper at the Summit House in Buckeye Hill, where her competence and severity make her respected and feared. Trotter, a poor and highly experienced working woman, nurses Chris Calton after he fractures his arm and collar-bone, while Calton becomes interested in the gentler chambermaid Frida Pauline Jansen. Frida’s attention helps Calton’s spirits during his recovery, and he returns to Roanoke Ledge after improving. He sends Trotter a valuable watch and chain in gratitude, while the nature of his gifts to Frida remains undisclosed.

l: Mr. Bilson, From Sand Hill to Pine, Mr. Bilson's Housekeeper
s: Joshua Bilson, of the Summit House, loses his wife and hires Miss Euphemia Trotter to manage the hotel with him. He stands in awe of Trotter, speaks of her with respect and reverence, and later is found in the card-room with Frida Pauline Jansen, offering an embarrassed and unconvincing explanation.

l: the Summit Hotel, From Sand Hill to Pine, Mr. Bilson's Housekeeper
s: The Summit House employs Miss Euphemia Trotter as housekeeper and receives Chris Calton as a patient after his injury. Calton convalesces there under medical supervision and Trotter’s care before returning to Roanoke Ledge.

l: Buckeye Hill, From Sand Hill to Pine, Mr. Bilson's Housekeeper
s: Buckeye Hill expects Joshua Bilson’s housekeeper to become his next wife, but is startled when he selects the serious, middle-aged, highly competent Miss Euphemia Trotter instead. The community respects and fears Trotter’s management of the hotel.

l: Miss Trotter, From Sand Hill to Pine, Mr. Bilson's Housekeeper
s: Miss Euphemia Trotter is a poor, hardworking woman who has been a teacher, hospital nurse, and reformatory assistant. As housekeeper, she supervises servants, examines bills and stores, and manages the Summit House with precision and authority. She nurses Chris Calton competently, adjusts his bandages, overlooks his interest in Frida Pauline Jansen, and receives a watch and chain from him in gratitude.

l: housekeeper employment, From Sand Hill to Pine, Mr. Bilson's Housekeeper
s: After his wife’s death, Joshua Bilson takes Miss Euphemia Trotter into the Summit House as housekeeper. Her employment is understood by the community as a practical appointment rather than a step toward marriage, and her work makes her respected, feared, and apparently influential over Bilson.

l: Frida Pauline Jansen, From Sand Hill to Pine, Mr. Bilson's Housekeeper
s: Frida Pauline Jansen is a pretty Swedish chambermaid at the Summit House. Miss Trotter sees her embracing an unfamiliar young man in the woods, and Frida later attends Chris Calton with gentleness and sympathy, receiving his admiration and apparently undisclosed gifts. She is also seen entering the gentlemen’s card-room, where Joshua Bilson is present.

l: Chris Calton, From Sand Hill to Pine, Mr. Bilson's Housekeeper
s: Chris Calton, a twenty-six-year-old partner in the Roanoke Ledge, is brought to the Summit House after fracturing his arm and collar-bone. He is emotional and initially despondent, but becomes especially appreciative of Frida Pauline Jansen’s gentleness and beauty. After recovering, he returns to Roanoke Ledge and sends Miss Trotter a watch and chain with a note of gratitude.

l: Dr. Duchesne, From Sand Hill to Pine, Mr. Bilson's Housekeeper
s: Dr. Duchesne directs Chris Calton’s treatment and asks Miss Euphemia Trotter to ensure that Calton eats properly, avoids excitement and worry, remains hopeful, and keeps his injured parts immobile. He praises Trotter’s nursing ability and believes she is largely responsible for Calton’s improvement, though he mistakenly interprets her look as suggesting that Calton is in love with her.

l: Calton's injury, From Sand Hill to Pine, Mr. Bilson's Housekeeper
s: Chris Calton fractures his arm and collar-bone in a fall. The injury is not comminuted, and Dr. Duchesne considers his constitution and blood healthy; the prescribed care consists of rest, proper food, limited company, emotional calm, and absolute immobility of the injured parts.

l: Calton's recovery, From Sand Hill to Pine, Mr. Bilson's Housekeeper
s: Chris Calton initially suffers despondency but later shows improved spirits and then sustained physical improvement. His bandages cause little trouble by the end of his stay, and he leaves the Summit House as a convalescent man to return to Roanoke Ledge.

l: medical nursing and convalescence, From Sand Hill to Pine, Mr. Bilson's Housekeeper
s: Miss Euphemia Trotter applies her previous hospital experience to Chris Calton’s care, following Dr. Duchesne’s directions and eventually replacing his splints herself when the surgeon fails to appear. Her precise nursing, together with rest and controlled company, supports Calton’s recovery at the Summit House.

l: romantic relationships and marriage, From Sand Hill to Pine, Mr. Bilson's Housekeeper
s: Buckeye Hill assumes that Bilson’s housekeeper will eventually become his wife, but Miss Euphemia Trotter shows no interest in that role. Frida Pauline Jansen is seen embracing an unidentified young man and later attracts Chris Calton’s admiration; the text also places Frida with Joshua Bilson in the card-room, but does not establish the nature of either relationship.

l: From Sand Hill to Pine, From Sand Hill to Pine, II One afternoon Miss Trotter received a message that Mr.
s: Jim Calton visits Miss Trotter to object to his brother Chris's engagement to Frida Jansen, arguing that Frida seeks Chris's wealth and is an unsuitable match. Miss Trotter rejects Jim's attempt to make her interfere, but later agrees to speak with Frida after Chris asks for her help. In the Summit woods, Chris sees Frida with Mr. Bilson and returns changed, releasing Miss Trotter from her promise after discovering her faithlessness. Mr. Bilson then tells Miss Trotter that he and Frida will marry, while Chris leaves without revealing the discovery to his brother.

l: Miss Trotter, From Sand Hill to Pine, II One afternoon Miss Trotter received a message that Mr.
s: Miss Trotter tells Jim Calton that she has no right to interfere with a guest's matrimonial intentions and refuses to condemn Frida's conduct without evidence that Frida has harmed her reputation. She agrees to speak with Frida at Chris's request, then discovers Frida with Mr. Bilson in the Summit woods. Although Mr. Bilson's marriage announcement will promote her to full control of the hotel, she feels troubled that her material success is connected with Chris's disappointment.

l: Chris Calton, From Sand Hill to Pine, II One afternoon Miss Trotter received a message that Mr.
s: Chris asks Miss Trotter to help preserve his relationship with Frida and promises not to see Frida until Miss Trotter has spoken with her. He goes to Frida before Miss Trotter can do so, discovers her with Mr. Bilson, and returns pale and changed, releasing Miss Trotter from her promise. He accepts his loss quietly and does not tell Jim what he has learned.

l: Jim Calton (Chris's elder brother), From Sand Hill to Pine, II One afternoon Miss Trotter received a message that Mr.
s: Jim visits Miss Trotter to oppose Chris's engagement to Frida, whom he considers an ignorant foreign servant seeking Chris's money. He believes Miss Trotter should control the girls' conduct and asks her to question Frida about what she expects from the marriage. Miss Trotter's reasoning leaves him discomfited, though he admires her clear-sightedness.

l: Frida Pauline Jansen, From Sand Hill to Pine, II One afternoon Miss Trotter received a message that Mr.
s: Frida is a yellow-haired foreigner employed at the hotel who has become engaged to Chris. In the Summit woods she is seen emerging from the pine grove with Mr. Bilson, displaying conscious, gratified vanity; Chris's discovery indicates that she has been unfaithful to him or was pursuing Mr. Bilson as well.

l: Mr. Bilson, From Sand Hill to Pine, II One afternoon Miss Trotter received a message that Mr.
s: Mr. Bilson is the proprietor of the hotel and is found privately with Frida in the Summit woods. He tells Miss Trotter that he intends to marry Frida in San Francisco and that their marriage will not diminish Miss Trotter's position, but will promote her to entire control of the establishment. He and Frida plan to go abroad after the wedding.

l: the Summit Hotel, From Sand Hill to Pine, II One afternoon Miss Trotter received a message that Mr.
s: The hotel employs Frida and places Miss Trotter in charge of ensuring that the girls perform their duties. After Mr. Bilson's marriage to Frida, Miss Trotter is to receive entire control of the establishment while the couple travels abroad.

l: Summit woods, From Sand Hill to Pine, II One afternoon Miss Trotter received a message that Mr.
s: The Summit woods are the setting for Miss Trotter's walk, her conversation with Chris, and Chris's discovery of Frida with Mr. Bilson. The woods recall Miss Trotter's earlier observations of Frida's flirtations and become the place where Chris learns of Frida's faithlessness.

l: Frida and Chris's engagement, From Sand Hill to Pine, II One afternoon Miss Trotter received a message that Mr.
s: Jim opposes Frida and Chris's engagement because he considers Frida unsuitable and suspects that she wants Chris's wealth. Chris asks Miss Trotter to help him maintain the engagement, but the engagement effectively collapses after he sees Frida with Mr. Bilson.

l: the marriage of Mr. Bilson and Frida, From Sand Hill to Pine, II One afternoon Miss Trotter received a message that Mr.
s: Mr. Bilson informs Miss Trotter that he and Frida will marry at once in San Francisco and then travel abroad for a year or two. Their marriage is presented as the outcome of Frida's relationship with Mr. Bilson and the cause of Chris's disappointment.

l: Chris's discovery of Frida's faithlessness, From Sand Hill to Pine, II One afternoon Miss Trotter received a message that Mr.
s: Chris discovers Frida with Mr. Bilson in the pine grove after going ahead to speak with her. He returns pale, older-looking, and emotionally controlled, refuses to explain what happened, and releases Miss Trotter from her promise to intervene.

l: marriage and romantic attachment, From Sand Hill to Pine, II One afternoon Miss Trotter received a message that Mr.
s: The unit contrasts Chris's sincere romantic attachment to Frida with Frida's apparent attachment to Mr. Bilson and the practical consequences of marriage. Miss Trotter reflects that Chris has been spared an ill-assorted marriage, while her own interest in him deepens only after his romantic defeat.

l: interference in the engagement, From Sand Hill to Pine, II One afternoon Miss Trotter received a message that Mr.
s: Jim asks Miss Trotter to interfere in Chris and Frida's engagement, but she argues that she has no authority over their personal intentions. Chris later voluntarily asks her to speak with Frida, though his discovery of Frida with Mr. Bilson makes her intervention unnecessary.

l: From Sand Hill to Pine, From Sand Hill to Pine, III When the news of the marriage reached Buckeye Hill, it did not, however, make much scandal, owing, possibly, to the scant number of the sex who are apt to disseminate it, and to many the name of Miss Jansen was unknown.
s: The news of Mr. Bilson’s marriage to Frida causes little scandal at Buckeye Hill, but Miss Trotter’s assumption of control of the Summit Hotel creates a stir. Chris Calton returns to the hotel after an illness and relapse, confesses that he never loved Frida, and declares his love for Miss Trotter. Miss Trotter resigns, leaves the Summit House, and later encounters Baroness X. at a foreign Spa, where she learns that Frida is now Mrs. Chris Calton. Miss Trotter leaves the Spa before Chris can return, and the nature of her relationship with him remains unresolved in the unit.

l: Miss Trotter, From Sand Hill to Pine, III When the news of the marriage reached Buckeye Hill, it did not, however, make much scandal, owing, possibly, to the scant number of the sex who are apt to disseminate it, and to many the name of Miss Jansen was unknown.
s: Miss Trotter becomes an independent woman of means and assumes superior control of the Summit Hotel while Mr. Bilson is absent. She learns that Chris Calton’s apparent courtship of Frida was a deception intended to provoke her attention, and he confesses his love to her. She later changes her dress and becomes less severe socially, resigns from the hotel, and leaves for a foreign Spa, where she avoids meeting Chris.

l: Chris Calton, From Sand Hill to Pine, III When the news of the marriage reached Buckeye Hill, it did not, however, make much scandal, owing, possibly, to the scant number of the sex who are apt to disseminate it, and to many the name of Miss Jansen was unknown.
s: Chris Calton returns to the Summit Hotel physically weakened after an illness and relapse. He explains to Miss Trotter that he never loved Frida, fabricated his apparent interest in her to gain Miss Trotter’s attention, and finally tells Miss Trotter that he loves her.

l: Jim Calton (Chris's elder brother), From Sand Hill to Pine, III When the news of the marriage reached Buckeye Hill, it did not, however, make much scandal, owing, possibly, to the scant number of the sex who are apt to disseminate it, and to many the name of Miss Jansen was unknown.
s: James Calton tells Miss Trotter that he believes her influence changed Chris and suggests that she see Chris while he is ill. He mistakenly implies that Chris may have transferred his affections to her, prompting Miss Trotter’s embarrassment.

l: Mr. Bilson, From Sand Hill to Pine, III When the news of the marriage reached Buckeye Hill, it did not, however, make much scandal, owing, possibly, to the scant number of the sex who are apt to disseminate it, and to many the name of Miss Jansen was unknown.
s: Mr. Bilson marries Frida and is absent from the Summit Hotel for a year. He later returns to take charge of the hotel after Miss Trotter resigns, and Miss Trotter sends him a letter addressed to Paris before that return.

l: Frida Pauline Jansen, From Sand Hill to Pine, III When the news of the marriage reached Buckeye Hill, it did not, however, make much scandal, owing, possibly, to the scant number of the sex who are apt to disseminate it, and to many the name of Miss Jansen was unknown.
s: Frida marries Mr. Bilson after Chris Calton’s apparent courtship of her ends. At the foreign Spa she is known as Mrs. Calton, having later married Chris Calton.

l: Buckeye Hill, From Sand Hill to Pine, III When the news of the marriage reached Buckeye Hill, it did not, however, make much scandal, owing, possibly, to the scant number of the sex who are apt to disseminate it, and to many the name of Miss Jansen was unknown.
s: Buckeye Hill reacts with little scandal to Mr. Bilson’s marriage, but its practical business community is stirred by Miss Trotter’s appointment to control the Summit Hotel. Its residents admire Miss Trotter’s social standing and later speculate about her possible marriage to Judge Boompointer or Judge Fletcher.

l: the Summit Hotel, From Sand Hill to Pine, III When the news of the marriage reached Buckeye Hill, it did not, however, make much scandal, owing, possibly, to the scant number of the sex who are apt to disseminate it, and to many the name of Miss Jansen was unknown.
s: The Summit Hotel comes under Miss Trotter’s superior control during Mr. Bilson’s absence. Chris Calton returns there to recover, and Miss Trotter later resigns so that Mr. Bilson can resume charge.

l: San Francisco, From Sand Hill to Pine, III When the news of the marriage reached Buckeye Hill, it did not, however, make much scandal, owing, possibly, to the scant number of the sex who are apt to disseminate it, and to many the name of Miss Jansen was unknown.
s: San Francisco is where Chris Calton plans to place himself under the care of a specialist. Miss Trotter tells the hotel housekeeper that this is the reason for his departure.

l: the foreign Spa, From Sand Hill to Pine, III When the news of the marriage reached Buckeye Hill, it did not, however, make much scandal, owing, possibly, to the scant number of the sex who are apt to disseminate it, and to many the name of Miss Jansen was unknown.
s: At a foreign Spa, Miss Trotter reappears three years later as a stately gray-haired stranger and is welcomed by Baroness X. She learns there that Frida is now Mrs. Chris Calton, then leaves before Chris returns from an excursion.

l: the marriage of Mr. Bilson and Frida, From Sand Hill to Pine, III When the news of the marriage reached Buckeye Hill, it did not, however, make much scandal, owing, possibly, to the scant number of the sex who are apt to disseminate it, and to many the name of Miss Jansen was unknown.
s: The marriage of Mr. Bilson and Frida produces little scandal at Buckeye Hill. Mr. Bilson’s absence leads to Miss Trotter’s temporary control of the Summit Hotel, and the couple later return after her resignation.

l: Chris Calton's illness and relapse, From Sand Hill to Pine, III When the news of the marriage reached Buckeye Hill, it did not, however, make much scandal, owing, possibly, to the scant number of the sex who are apt to disseminate it, and to many the name of Miss Jansen was unknown.
s: Chris Calton suffers a relapse after being careless during his convalescence and experiences renewed trouble with his arm. James Calton says that Chris is off his feed and persuades him to return to the Summit Hotel, where Miss Trotter watches over his recovery.

l: Chris Calton's confession of love, From Sand Hill to Pine, III When the news of the marriage reached Buckeye Hill, it did not, however, make much scandal, owing, possibly, to the scant number of the sex who are apt to disseminate it, and to many the name of Miss Jansen was unknown.
s: Chris Calton confesses to Miss Trotter that his apparent love for Frida was a scheme arising from his admiration for Miss Trotter and his desire for her attention. He ends the confession by taking Miss Trotter’s hands and saying, "Because I love you."

l: Miss Trotter's resignation, From Sand Hill to Pine, III When the news of the marriage reached Buckeye Hill, it did not, however, make much scandal, owing, possibly, to the scant number of the sex who are apt to disseminate it, and to many the name of Miss Jansen was unknown.
s: Miss Trotter resigns from the Summit Hotel because she needs a complete change. Her resignation permits Mr. Bilson to return and take charge of the hotel.

l: Miss Trotter's departure from the Summit House, From Sand Hill to Pine, III When the news of the marriage reached Buckeye Hill, it did not, however, make much scandal, owing, possibly, to the scant number of the sex who are apt to disseminate it, and to many the name of Miss Jansen was unknown.
s: After resigning, Miss Trotter takes her holiday and leaves the Summit House, which no longer knows her. Three years later she is living and traveling at a foreign Spa.

l: Miss Trotter and Chris Calton's relationship, From Sand Hill to Pine, III When the news of the marriage reached Buckeye Hill, it did not, however, make much scandal, owing, possibly, to the scant number of the sex who are apt to disseminate it, and to many the name of Miss Jansen was unknown.
s: Chris Calton’s confession reveals that he has long admired Miss Trotter and used his supposed attachment to Frida to provoke her concern. Miss Trotter is deeply affected by the confession, but she leaves the Summit House and later departs the foreign Spa before meeting Chris again; the unit does not state that they marry or otherwise settle their relationship.

l: Laurence Sterne in Germany, Laurence Sterne in Germany, NEW YORK, May 1, 1905.
s: The introduction examines Germany’s literary dependence on foreign models, especially the predominant English influence in the latter half of the eighteenth century. It explains how English writers, translations, periodicals, and the English novel helped shape German fiction, particularly through Robinson Crusoe, Richardson, Rousseau, and Fielding. The German novel is described as constrained by pedantry, pedagogy, and theoretical speculation, while English narrative fiction offered models of everyday life, feeling, action, and humor. The unit presents Laurence Sterne’s reception in Germany as an example of widespread popularity, imitation, and opposition arising from concerns about originality and national literary independence.

l: German culture, Laurence Sterne in Germany, NEW YORK, May 1, 1905.
s: German culture is described as having benefited from contact with other peoples, especially England during the latter half of the eighteenth century. English models helped awaken Germany to its own cultural possibilities.

l: German literature, Laurence Sterne in Germany, NEW YORK, May 1, 1905.
s: German literature is presented as developing through successive connections with foreign literatures, with English influence becoming predominant in the latter half of the eighteenth century. The period is characterized by extensive reading, translation, imitation, and debate over originality.

l: English influence in Germany, Laurence Sterne in Germany, NEW YORK, May 1, 1905.
s: English influence in Germany spread through moral weeklies, religious and didactic poetry, literary journals, translations, and the popularity of English authors. It helped shape German tastes while allowing more independence than the earlier dominance of French models.

l: English literary interests, Laurence Sterne in Germany, NEW YORK, May 1, 1905.
s: English literature supplied Germany with influential authors and literary movements, including Robinson Crusoe, Richardson, Fielding, and Edward Young. English works were read in the original and in numerous popular translations.

l: German imitation of English literature, Laurence Sterne in Germany, NEW YORK, May 1, 1905.
s: German imitation of English literature became widespread as a result of admiration for English models. Some German works even presented themselves as translations from English because that designation attracted readers.

l: Sentimental Journey, Laurence Sterne in Germany, NEW YORK, May 1, 1905.
s: The Sentimental Journey is identified in the contents as the subject of chapters concerning its publication and Sterne’s reception before and after publication. The introduction presents Sterne’s story in Germany as an example of popularity, imitation, and opposition.

l: Laurence Sterne, Laurence Sterne in Germany, NEW YORK, May 1, 1905.
s: Laurence Sterne is introduced as the central example of an English author whose work produced sweeping popularity, servile admiration, extensive imitation, and opposition in Germany.

l: Sterne’s influence in Germany, Laurence Sterne in Germany, NEW YORK, May 1, 1905.
s: Sterne's influence in Germany is framed as an individual instance of the broader English influence on German literature. The document’s contents indicate that this influence will be examined before and after the publication of The Sentimental Journey.

l: imitators of Sterne, Laurence Sterne in Germany, NEW YORK, May 1, 1905.
s: Imitators of Sterne are identified in the contents as a major subject of the study. The introduction places their activity within Germany’s broader tendency to imitate admired English authors and literary movements.

l: opposition to Sterne and his type of sentimentalism, Laurence Sterne in Germany, NEW YORK, May 1, 1905.
s: Opposition to Sterne and his type of sentimentalism is identified in the contents as a separate subject. The introduction connects such opposition with German concerns about foreign imitation, national limitations, and the need for independent literary ideals.

l: the English novel, Laurence Sterne in Germany, NEW YORK, May 1, 1905.
s: The English novel is described as a decisive influence on the development of German fiction. Robinson Crusoe connected the extraordinary with everyday life, Richardson emphasized the analysis of human sensibilities, and Fielding strengthened the representation of real and ordinary life while opposing excessive emotionalism.

l: the German novel, Laurence Sterne in Germany, NEW YORK, May 1, 1905.
s: The German novel is portrayed as having moved beyond wild, extraordinary, and grotesque tales under the influence of classicism and growing interest in middle-class life. It remained burdened by pedantry, pedagogy, and theoretical speculation, often becoming a mirror of opinions about life rather than a consequential representation of events and character.

l: England, Laurence Sterne in Germany, NEW YORK, May 1, 1905.
s: England is presented as the leading source of literary models for Germany during the latter half of the eighteenth century. Its social conditions were regarded by several German commentators as especially favorable to individual development, humor, eccentricity, and novelistic material.

l: Germany, Laurence Sterne in Germany, NEW YORK, May 1, 1905.
s: Germany is described as heavily dependent on foreign literary models while gradually seeking independent national ideals. Its literature was considered less favorable than England’s to humor and vigorous narrative because of political, social, and intellectual constraints.

l: Empfindsamkeit, Laurence Sterne in Germany, NEW YORK, May 1, 1905.
s: Sentimentalism appears in the discussion of Richardson’s intense analysis of human sensibilities and in the contents’ reference to Sterne’s type of sentimentalism. The unit presents emotional expression as one of the literary interests imported and debated in Germany.

l: originality in German literature, Laurence Sterne in Germany, NEW YORK, May 1, 1905.
s: Originality in German literature became a major concern as thinkers reacted to successive periods of foreign dependence. Edward Young’s Conjectures on Original Composition and Herder’s complaints about the scarcity of originals and geniuses contributed to this debate.

l: German national identity, Laurence Sterne in Germany, NEW YORK, May 1, 1905.
s: German national identity is connected with the effort to transform foreign influence into independent cultural achievement. English study is said to have helped Germany recognize its own inherent possibilities even as imitation raised fears of national limitation or disintegration.

l: Sterne imitation in German literature, Laurence Sterne in Germany, NEW YORK, May 1, 1905.

Johann Joachim Christoph Bode is identified as the probable translator of several Hamburg volumes, whose work was generally praised by German reviewers. It also traces German translations and misattributions of Sterne’s sermons and other spurious works, including “Sermons to Asses,” Yorick’s meditations, and The Koran. German criticism often accepted works as Sterne’s despite doubts about their authenticity, helping shape the German image of Yorick.

l: Laurence Sterne, Laurence Sterne in Germany, Naturally Sterne’s letters found readers in Germany, the Yorick-Eliza correspond
s: Laurence Sterne’s letters, sermons, novels, and purportedly posthumous works received extensive attention in Germany. German translations and criticism sometimes praised works as his despite substantial doubts or demonstrable errors of attribution.

l: Yorick, Laurence Sterne in Germany, Naturally Sterne’s letters found readers in Germany, the Yorick-Eliza correspond
s: Yorick was presented in Germany as a sentimental, benevolent, and morally restrained figure, especially through the Yorick-Eliza letters. Spurious works and translations further shaped the German conception of Yorick, sometimes portraying him as an opponent of oppression and arbitrary power.

l: Eliza, Laurence Sterne in Germany, Naturally Sterne’s letters found readers in Germany, the Yorick-Eliza correspond
s: Eliza was the subject of a widely translated correspondence with Yorick. German publications presented letters from Eliza and letters to her, while reviewers debated the authenticity and moral character of the relationship.

l: Bode, Laurence Sterne in Germany, Naturally Sterne’s letters found readers in Germany, the Yorick-Eliza correspond
s: Johann Joachim Christoph Bode is identified as the probable translator of the 1775 Hamburg volumes containing Yorick’s letters to Eliza, letters from Eliza, and miscellaneous letters. His translations were praised by German reviewers, and his translator’s notes show an intention to render Sterne’s writings and related materials into German.

l: German readers, Laurence Sterne in Germany, Naturally Sterne’s letters found readers in Germany, the Yorick-Eliza correspond
s: German readers showed strong interest in Sterne’s letters, especially the Yorick-Eliza correspondence. They also encountered numerous translations and purported works that were more extensively recognized in Germany than in England.

l: Germany, Laurence Sterne in Germany, Naturally Sterne’s letters found readers in Germany, the Yorick-Eliza correspond
s: Germany received translations, reviews, and imitations of Sterne’s letters, sermons, novels, and spurious writings. German criticism often accepted questionable works as genuine or treated them sympathetically, thereby contributing to a distinctive German image of Yorick.

l: Hamburg, Laurence Sterne in Germany, Naturally Sterne’s letters found readers in Germany, the Yorick-Eliza correspond
s: Hamburg was the site of several 1775 editions of the Yorick-Eliza letters and related collections. These editions were probably translated by Bode and were reviewed favorably, with Bode’s version preferred over another translation.

l: “Letters from Yorick to Eliza”, Laurence Sterne in Germany, Naturally Sterne’s letters found readers in Germany, the Yorick-Eliza correspond
s: The English edition of “Letters from Yorick to Eliza” was reviewed in German journals and translated in Hamburg in 1775. German reviewers discussed its tenderness, moral character, and authenticity, while Bode’s translation received particular praise.

l: Yorick-Eliza correspondence, Laurence Sterne in Germany, Naturally Sterne’s letters found readers in Germany, the Yorick-Eliza correspond
s: The Yorick-Eliza correspondence was especially successful with German readers. Reviewers generally regarded the relationship as extraordinarily tender but Platonic, although some questioned whether the letters were original or genuine.

l: Sermons of Mr. Yorick, Laurence Sterne in Germany, Naturally Sterne’s letters found readers in Germany, the Yorick-Eliza correspond
s: Sterne’s sermons were translated and reviewed in Germany but were less popular than his novels. A Leipzig translation appeared in 1770, and later commentary praised the sermons while sometimes attaching inaccurate information about Sterne and the English church to them.

l: “Sermons to Asses”, Laurence Sterne in Germany, Naturally Sterne’s letters found readers in Germany, the Yorick-Eliza correspond
s: “Sermons to Asses” was mistakenly associated with Sterne in some German publications and translations. The work was actually written by Rev. James Murray and directed against the established church, taxation, and coercive power.

l: Sentimental Journey, Laurence Sterne in Germany, Naturally Sterne’s letters found readers in Germany, the Yorick-Eliza correspond
s: The Sentimental Journey was treated by German critics as superior to the spurious or doubtful works attributed to Sterne. Yorick’s Meditations was placed below the Sentimental Journey and below Tristram Shandy, though above many artificial works then popular.

l: Tristram Shandy, Laurence Sterne in Germany, Naturally Sterne’s letters found readers in Germany, the Yorick-Eliza correspond
s: Tristram Shandy served as a standard against which German critics compared Sterne’s genuine and purported works. Yorick’s Meditations was judged inferior to it, and the Koran was evaluated in relation to Yorick’s other writings.

l: Koran, Laurence Sterne in Germany, Naturally Sterne’s letters found readers in Germany, the Yorick-Eliza correspond
s: The Koran was a purportedly posthumous work that English critics considered manifestly spurious, but it received considerably greater recognition in Germany. German translations appeared in 1771 and 1778, and several German reviewers accepted or warmly praised it despite acknowledging, in some cases, doubts about its authorship.

l: Platonic affection, Laurence Sterne in Germany, Naturally Sterne’s letters found readers in Germany, the Yorick-Eliza correspond
s: Platonic affection was the interpretation German reviewers applied to the tenderness of the Yorick-Eliza relationship. They argued that virtue and rectitude were preserved despite the correspondence’s emotional warmth.

l: authenticity of Sterne’s letters, Laurence Sterne in Germany, Naturally Sterne’s letters found readers in Germany, the Yorick-Eliza correspond
s: The authenticity of Sterne’s letters was repeatedly debated in Germany. Some reviewers accepted the Yorick-Eliza letters as genuine, while others suspected that particular letters or collections were fabricated, including letters later identified by a confessedly spurious 1780 collection as imitations.

l: “Sermons to Asses” authorship controversy, Laurence Sterne in Germany, Naturally Sterne’s letters found readers in Germany, the Yorick-Eliza correspond
s: The “Sermons to Asses” authorship controversy arose because German translations and criticism attributed the work to Sterne. The unit states that Rev. James Murray was its actual author and suggests that the German attribution resulted from ignorance, imitation, or a one-sided understanding of Sterne.

l: Laurence Sterne in Germany, Laurence Sterne in Germany, Sterne’s unacknowledged borrowings, his high-handed and extensive appropriation
s: The unit examines Laurence Sterne’s extensive unacknowledged borrowings and the largely moderate German response to them. George Ferriar’s investigations became known in Germany chiefly through Friedrich Nicolai’s 1795 summary, which defended Sterne’s creative adaptation, while Gotthold Ephraim Lessing had apparently noticed similar borrowings but remained silent. The unit also traces English imitations of Sterne, especially works modeled on the Sentimental Journey, and their German translations or adaptations. These included imitations attributed to Samuel Paterson, Schink, and others, as well as works presented as continuations or companions to Yorick’s travels.

l: Laurence Sterne, Laurence Sterne in Germany, Sterne’s unacknowledged borrowings, his high-handed and extensive appropriation
s: Laurence Sterne was criticized for extensive, unacknowledged appropriation of material from other writers, especially Burton’s Anatomy of Melancholy. Friedrich Nicolai nevertheless argued that Sterne’s additions, alterations, personal tone, Empfindsamkeit, and Laune made him more than a brainless copyist and that investigating his sources did not depreciate him.

l: Sterne’s unacknowledged borrowings, Laurence Sterne in Germany, Sterne’s unacknowledged borrowings, his high-handed and extensive appropriation
s: Sterne’s unacknowledged borrowings were noted in Germany as a result of George Ferriar’s investigations in England, but they did not seriously damage Sterne’s standing among his admirers. The subject remained an unavoidable element of English discussions of Sterne and his place in literature.

l: George Ferriar, Laurence Sterne in Germany, Sterne’s unacknowledged borrowings, his high-handed and extensive appropriation
s: George Ferriar investigated Sterne’s borrowings and presented passages from Burton’s Anatomy of Melancholy as evidence of Sterne’s theft. Friedrich Nicolai gave his findings a favorable and measured presentation in Germany, while Lichtenberg attacked Sterne more spitefully in connection with Ferriar’s essay.

l: Germany, Laurence Sterne in Germany, Sterne’s unacknowledged borrowings, his high-handed and extensive appropriation
s: Germany learned about Ferriar’s investigations mainly through Friedrich Nicolai’s résumé in the Berlinische Monatsschrift in 1795, since Ferriar’s book and the original Manchester society papers apparently were not reprinted or translated. German readers also encountered numerous English imitations of Sterne, particularly works modeled on the Sentimental Journey.

l: England, Laurence Sterne in Germany, Sterne’s unacknowledged borrowings, his high-handed and extensive appropriation
s: England was the setting for Ferriar’s investigations and for continuing debate over Sterne’s borrowings. It also produced numerous imitations, continuations, explanations, and protests connected with Sterne, several of which later reached Germany.

l: Gotthold Ephraim Lessing, Laurence Sterne in Germany, Sterne’s unacknowledged borrowings, his high-handed and extensive appropriation
s: Gotthold Ephraim Lessing possessed a copy of Burton’s Anatomy of Melancholy containing marks beside several passages that Ferriar later cited as evidence of Sterne’s theft. Although Lessing evidently recognized the borrowings, he remained silent about them.

l: Nicolai, Laurence Sterne in Germany, Sterne’s unacknowledged borrowings, his high-handed and extensive appropriation
s: Friedrich Nicolai summarized Ferriar’s findings in the February 1795 issue of the Berlinische Monatsschrift. He defended Sterne as a refined, ingenious, and humorous author whose creative additions and distinctive qualities justified his reputation, and he maintained that source investigations should explain rather than depreciate him.

l: Yorick, Laurence Sterne in Germany, Sterne’s unacknowledged borrowings, his high-handed and extensive appropriation
s: Yorick served as the central figure and stylistic model for many German translations and imitations of the Sentimental Journey. Works were published as journeys in Yorick’s manner, as continuations of his travels, or as productions associated with his supposed son, while one later title presented itself as a fifth volume of Yorick’s Empfindsame Reisen.

l: Tristram Shandy, Laurence Sterne in Germany, Sterne’s unacknowledged borrowings, his high-handed and extensive appropriation
s: Tristram Shandy was identified by Friedrich Nicolai as evidence of Sterne’s rich creative adaptation of borrowed material. Nicolai argued that the creator of Tristram Shandy compensated for a lack of learning through observation, thought, feeling, and original treatment.

l: Sentimental Journey, Laurence Sterne in Germany, Sterne’s unacknowledged borrowings, his high-handed and extensive appropriation
s: The Sentimental Journey was the principal Sterne work imitated in the English productions that reached Germany. German versions and adaptations included Empfindsame Reisen durch einen Theil der Niederlande, Die neue empfindsame Reise in Yoriks Geschmack, and Schink’s Empfindsame Reisen durch Italien, die Schweiz und Frankreich.

l: English imitations of Sterne, Laurence Sterne in Germany, Sterne’s unacknowledged borrowings, his high-handed and extensive appropriation
s: English imitations of Sterne reached Germany and were often grouped indiscriminately with the broader mass of Yorick production and influence. They included Samuel Paterson’s Another Traveller, Peter Pennyless, continuations of the Sentimental Journey, A Sentimental Journey intended as a sequel, and Fragments in the manner of Sterne, which were translated, adapted, or reprinted in German.

l: Laurence Sterne in Germany, Laurence Sterne in Germany, ] CHAPTER V STERNE’S INFLUENCE IN GERMANY Thus in manifold ways Sterne was introduced into German life and letters.
s: The unit describes Sterne’s broad influence in Germany, where he was regarded as a humane guide, emotional mentor, and model for conduct as well as literature. Johann Georg Jacobi’s “Lorenzodosen,” horn snuff-boxes associated with Yorick and Franciscan Lorenzo, became a popular sentimental fad and inspired proposed orders and rituals. Sterne’s influence also shaped German attitudes toward animals, travel writing, humor, whimsy, and literary imitation. Wieland absorbed Sterne’s style and motifs in several works while remaining an independent thinker who later criticized slavish imitation of Sterne.

l: Laurence Sterne, Laurence Sterne in Germany, ] CHAPTER V STERNE’S INFLUENCE IN GERMANY Thus in manifold ways Sterne was introduced into German life and letters.
s: Sterne was introduced into German life and letters as a figure of benignant humanity, sympathy, emotional expression, and practical moral guidance. His influence appeared in conduct, sentimental customs, travel writing, humor, and numerous German literary imitations, although the unit distinguishes independent engagement from slavish imitation.

l: Sterne’s influence in Germany, Laurence Sterne in Germany, ] CHAPTER V STERNE’S INFLUENCE IN GERMANY Thus in manifold ways Sterne was introduced into German life and letters.
s: Sterne’s influence in Germany extended beyond literature into social conduct and sentimental rituals, including the Lorenzodosen and proposed orders devoted to gentleness and reconciliation. It also encouraged more personal and humorous travel narratives, sympathy toward animals, and imitation of Sterne’s whimsical style.

l: Germany, Laurence Sterne in Germany, ] CHAPTER V STERNE’S INFLUENCE IN GERMANY Thus in manifold ways Sterne was introduced into German life and letters.
s: Germany accorded Sterne the honors and influence of a foreign cultural figure, treating him as a prophet, mentor, and authority on emotional and humane conduct. His works and associated customs spread through Germany and even reached Denmark and Livonia.

l: Yorick, Laurence Sterne in Germany, ] CHAPTER V STERNE’S INFLUENCE IN GERMANY Thus in manifold ways Sterne was introduced into German life and letters.
s: Yorick was judged in Germany to be a preceptor whose teachings could modify human relationships and conduct. His treatment of Franciscan Lorenzo, his sympathy for animals, and his sentimental and whimsical manner inspired customs, literary imitations, and discussions of travel and emotional expression.

l: Lorenzodosen, Laurence Sterne in Germany, ] CHAPTER V STERNE’S INFLUENCE IN GERMANY Thus in manifold ways Sterne was introduced into German life and letters.
s: Lorenzodosen were horn snuff-boxes bearing “Pater Lorenzo” on the outside and “Yorick” within, created to commemorate the emotional response to Sterne’s story of Franciscan Lorenzo. They became a widespread fad, were manufactured and sold commercially, and were associated with an oath to practice gentleness and restrain anger.

l: Jacobi, Laurence Sterne in Germany, ] CHAPTER V STERNE’S INFLUENCE IN GERMANY Thus in manifold ways Sterne was introduced into German life and letters.
s: Johann Georg Jacobi introduced the Lorenzodosen after reading Sterne’s account of Franciscan Lorenzo with his brother and several ladies. He explained the custom in an open letter to Gleim, promoted its spread among friends, and later noted that merchants had turned it into a commercial speculation.

l: Sentimental Journey, Laurence Sterne in Germany, ] CHAPTER V STERNE’S INFLUENCE IN GERMANY Thus in manifold ways Sterne was introduced into German life and letters.
s: The Sentimental Journey supplied the story of the poor Franciscan whose snuff-box inspired Jacobi and his companions to create the Lorenzodosen. Its account of Yorick’s sympathy also provided a model for German discussions of humane conduct and animal feeling.

l: Lorenzo, Laurence Sterne in Germany, ] CHAPTER V STERNE’S INFLUENCE IN GERMANY Thus in manifold ways Sterne was introduced into German life and letters.
s: Franciscan Lorenzo was honored by Jacobi and his companions as a model of gentleness, contentment, invincible patience, and forgiveness. They believed he deserved canonization more than the saints of the calendar and associated his memory with the Lorenzodosen.

l: Christoph Martin Wieland, Laurence Sterne in Germany, ] CHAPTER V STERNE’S INFLUENCE IN GERMANY Thus in manifold ways Sterne was introduced into German life and letters.
s: Wieland was one of Sterne’s most ardent admirers and intelligent interpreters, and Sterne’s style and motifs appear in several of Wieland’s works from 1768 to 1774. Wieland later continued to call Sterne the author from whom he would last part, while protesting against foolish and unsuccessful imitation of Sterne.

l: Johann Wolfgang Goethe, Laurence Sterne in Germany, ] CHAPTER V STERNE’S INFLUENCE IN GERMANY Thus in manifold ways Sterne was introduced into German life and letters.
s: Goethe is mentioned as the friend of Fritz Jacobi and as an author who later acknowledged an impulse from Yorick in his account of travel in the “Campagne in Frankreich.” The unit also notes that Goethe satirized Leuchsenring in “Pater Brey.”

l: Tristram Shandy, Laurence Sterne in Germany, ] CHAPTER V STERNE’S INFLUENCE IN GERMANY Thus in manifold ways Sterne was introduced into German life and letters.
s: Tristram Shandy contributed characters and motifs to German sentimental and eccentric culture, including Uncle Toby and Corporal Trim in the imagined cemetery at Marienwerder. Its Shandean style of narration was adopted in German novels dealing with middle-class domestic life, and Wieland later discussed a failed novel written in its style.

l: Laurence Sterne in Germany, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [37] Herder’s early acquaintance with Sterne has been already treated.
s: The unit examines Laurence Sterne’s continuing influence on German writers, especially Johann Wolfgang Goethe, while also discussing Johann Gottfried Herder and Gotthold Ephraim Lessing. It traces Goethe’s early exposure to Sterne in Strassburg, his later references to Sterne, possible parallels between their works, and Goethe’s explicit statements of indebtedness. It also investigates Goethe’s use of material from The Koran in Wilhelm Meister’s Journeyman Years and considers whether this constituted literary plagiarism. The unit concludes that Goethe’s relationship to Sterne involved admiration and cultural assimilation more than easily demonstrable direct imitation.

l: Johann Gottfried Herder, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [37] Herder’s early acquaintance with Sterne has been already treated.
s: Johann Gottfried Herder continued to admire Laurence Sterne after his early acquaintance with him. Soon after arriving in Paris, he praised Sterne’s characterization of the French people to Hartknoch, and his fifth “Wäldchen” refers to Sterne.

l: Laurence Sterne, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [37] Herder’s early acquaintance with Sterne has been already treated.
s: Laurence Sterne is presented as an important influence on eighteenth-century German writers, particularly through his humor, sentiment, tolerance, and attacks on pedantry and philistinism. Johann Wolfgang Goethe repeatedly expressed admiration for Sterne and returned to reading his works late in life.

l: Johann Wolfgang Goethe, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [37] Herder’s early acquaintance with Sterne has been already treated.
s: Johann Wolfgang Goethe first seems to have read Laurence Sterne’s works in Strassburg under Johann Gottfried Herder’s guidance. He later recommended Sterne to Jung-Stilling, read the story of poor Le Fevre aloud to the Darmstadt circle, referred to Sterne in letters and conversations, and acknowledged being infinitely indebted to Shakespeare, Sterne, and Goldsmith. Goethe also used or reproduced material associated with Sterne and The Koran in Wilhelm Meister’s Journeyman Years.

l: Johann Peter Eckermann, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [37] Herder’s early acquaintance with Sterne has been already treated.
s: Johann Peter Eckermann recorded several of Johann Wolfgang Goethe’s statements about Laurence Sterne. Goethe compared Eckermann to a second Shandy, while Eckermann discussed Sterne’s descriptions and ideas in conversation with Goethe.

l: Yorick, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [37] Herder’s early acquaintance with Sterne has been already treated.
s: Yorick is treated as a central vehicle for Laurence Sterne’s influence on German literature. Johann Wolfgang Goethe said that Yorick helped prepare the sentimental ground on which The Sorrows of Young Werther was built, and he later called Yorick Sterne a uniquely liberating and beautiful spirit.

l: Tristram Shandy, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [37] Herder’s early acquaintance with Sterne has been already treated.
s: Tristram Shandy was read aloud by Johann Wolfgang Goethe to the Darmstadt circle less than a year after his departure from Strassburg, specifically through the story of poor Le Fevre. Goethe also invoked Walter Shandy’s failure to attend to a squeaking door-hinge when comparing Johann Peter Eckermann to a second Shandy.

l: Sentimental Journey, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [37] Herder’s early acquaintance with Sterne has been already treated.
s: A Sentimental Journey Through France and Italy influenced the way travel writing was associated with the feelings and opinions of the traveler. Johann Wolfgang Goethe stated that he later tried to keep his own travel accounts objective, rather than follow the sentimental approach he attributed to Sterne.

l: The Sorrows of Young Werther, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [37] Herder’s early acquaintance with Sterne has been already treated.
s: The Sorrows of Young Werther contains no direct influence from Laurence Sterne that the unit can demonstrate, but it reflects a mental and emotional condition to which Sterne contributed. Johann Wolfgang Goethe later said that Yorick helped prepare the sentimental groundwork on which Werther was built.

l: Wilhelm Meister’s Journeyman Years, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [37] Herder’s early acquaintance with Sterne has been already treated.
s: Wilhelm Meister’s Journeyman Years included appendices containing miscellaneous sayings and reflections, among them material taken from The Koran and comments on Laurence Sterne. The material was added when the publisher found that the final two volumes were too thin, and it was later reprinted among Goethe’s posthumous works.

l: Koran, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [37] Herder’s early acquaintance with Sterne has been already treated.
s: The Koran was identified as the source of twenty sayings and reflections printed in the appendix to Wilhelm Meister’s Journeyman Years. It was also considered a possible source for the story of the Graf von Gleichen, which may have contributed to Johann Wolfgang Goethe’s Stella.

l: German literature, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [37] Herder’s early acquaintance with Sterne has been already treated.
s: German literature increasingly possessed native worth that may have overshadowed Laurence Sterne’s influence on writers such as Johann Gottfried Herder and Gotthold Ephraim Lessing. The unit nevertheless presents Sterne as a force in extending literary conventions and shaping German sentimental culture.

l: Empfindsamkeit, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [37] Herder’s early acquaintance with Sterne has been already treated.
s: Sentimentalism provided the emotional and intellectual ground on which The Sorrows of Young Werther was built. Johann Wolfgang Goethe associated Laurence Sterne and Yorick with the preparation of this ground, while distinguishing Sterne’s whim and sentiment from Goethe’s own treatment.

l: Goethe’s indebtedness to Sterne, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [37] Herder’s early acquaintance with Sterne has been already treated.
s: Goethe’s indebtedness to Sterne is expressed directly in his statement that he was infinitely indebted to Shakespeare, Sterne, and Goldsmith. He also described Sterne’s influence as formative at the chief point of his development and praised Sterne’s irony, broad outlook, gentleness toward opposition, and equanimity.
